text: Receivables mirrors everything you just learned on the Payables side — same chaining logic, different tables. Customer, transaction, cash receipt, and a linking table in between.

Four tables: H-Z Cust Accounts for the customer's account, R-A Customer Trx All for a transaction to that customer, A-R Receivable Applications All linking a payment schedule to the cash that paid it, and A-R Cash Receipts All for the actual money that came in.

Why does "customer" split into its own account table? Fusion keeps a customer's identity separate from their account relationship with you. Select account number, transaction number, transaction date. From cust accounts, inner join customer trx all, on bill-to-customer-id equals cust-account-id.

Now chain further. Transaction, to payment schedules, to receivable applications, to the cash receipt itself. Notice applications doesn't join straight to the transaction — it joins through the payment schedule's own ID, because its whole job is tracking how much of that specific schedule has been applied.

Four tables, four ON conditions — exactly the same chaining principle from the Payables join in lesson 7. Different table names, same mental model: start at the customer, chain forward link by link to the money.
Receivables isn't a new skill — it's the same joins, aimed at a mirror set of tables. Next lesson: journals, ledgers, and periods, on the General Ledger side.
